1.pericope_label: My son, if thou wilt receive my words: if thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures

schools.summary: Henry sets the chapter against the older question where wisdom may be found, which was answered only by saying that God knows the place of it, and holds that this teacher goes further by telling both where it is and how to get it; he breaks the means into five and insists that though many wise things are found in human compositions, divine revelation and the religion built on it are all wisdom.

Gill reads wisdom throughout as Christ and the instruction offered as the Gospel, takes the fear of the Lord for a grace wrought in the heart rather than a lesson learned, and makes the hiding of the words the laying up of a treasure.

Clarke turns the command to hide the words into a rule about character, that a man whose duty lies only in his Bible and his head cannot be steady since his obedience is forced, while the man with the word in his heart works from his heart; he illustrates the search for wisdom from slaves washing a river bed for diamonds under a law granting freedom to the finder of a large one, so precious is liberty to the human heart. Wesley reads the hiding as laying up a choicest treasure.

Ellicott proves that mining was understood long before the book’s reputed date from copper mines in one peninsula and gold mines in a desert, with rock inscriptions dated four thousand years before our era, and explains the hidden treasure from the insecurity of property that made buried hoards frequent and hunting for them a keen interest; he also makes the knowledge of God the highest of gifts while noting an apostle preferred to speak of being known by him. Keil and Delitzsch derive the verb for searching from the primary meaning of a ditch and report an old rabbinic direction to read the third verse otherwise.

outliers: Clarke illustrates the search for wisdom from slaves employed to wash the soil of a river bed for gold and diamonds, under a law by which whoever finds a diamond of a certain weight receives his freedom, and says that whoever succeeds in the search he recommends finds the liberty of the children of God.

Ellicott dates the plausibility of the mining figure from copper mines in one peninsula and gold mines in a desert, with rock inscriptions near the first placed by one scholar four thousand years before our era.
Keil and Delitzsch report an old rabbinic direction to read the third verse otherwise than it stands, so that the sense becomes if thou callest understanding mother, and set the reading aside.

Ellicott explains the hidden treasure from the frequency of burying wealth where life and property were insecure, and from owners dying without disclosing the place, which made hunting for such hoards a standing interest and furnished the ground of a Gospel parable.
themes: a question asked in an older book and answered here
the heart required as well as the head
wisdom sought with the diligence of a treasure-hunter
a metaphor tested against the history of mining
knowledge of God confessed to be partial even at its highest

6.pericope_label: For the Lord giveth wisdom: he layeth up sound wisdom for the righteous

schools.summary: Gill notes that the giving of wisdom is declared here partly to caution seekers against crediting their own diligence, reports two Jewish commentators making the sound wisdom the law and rejects that for the Gospel, gives the philological sense as essence or substance, and allows the eighth verse to be rendered as stating the effect of God’s being a buckler rather than a separate act.

Clarke confesses that it is hard to find in any language a term proper for the word rendered sound wisdom, takes it as the essence or substance of a thing and quotes an older English version rendering the clause of preserving the welfare of the righteous, and closes by repeating his rule that a man taught of God has the law written on his heart while one who understands these things by books only will never practise or profit by them; Wesley allows that keeping paths may stand for keeping men in their paths.

Ellicott glosses the giving of wisdom from a later writer’s liberally and upbraideth not, renders the disputed term as furtherance or advancement against the sense of essence, takes the eighth verse of God protecting those who walk in the paths, and traces the word rendered saints from its use in the law of the tribe set apart for service, through its frequency in the Psalter, to its adoption as a party name in the time of the Maccabees by those devoted to the law against the friends of Greek culture.

debates: What is sound wisdom? Gill reports two Jewish commentators making it the law because it endures when all else fails, rejects that for the Gospel, and gives the philological sense as essence or substance; Clarke agrees with that last, confesses it hard to find a proper term in any language, and takes it as the thing itself, that which is chief of its kind; Ellicott renders it literally furtherance or advancement instead.

Who keeps the paths of judgment? Gill allows the words to be rendered as an infinitive so that the clause states the effect of God’s being a buckler rather than a further act of his; Ellicott takes the plain sense that God protects those who walk in them; Wesley allows that keeping paths may stand for keeping men in their paths.
outliers: Ellicott traces the word rendered saints from the law, where it describes a tribe set apart for its zeal in God’s service, through its frequency in the Psalter, to the time of the Maccabees when it was taken as a party name by those voluntarily devoted to the law against the friends of Greek religion and culture.
Clarke confesses openly that no language supplies a proper term for the word rendered sound wisdom, and settles for the essence or substance of a thing, that which is chief of its kind.
Gill observes that the declaration that God gives wisdom is placed here to caution those who seek and find it against attributing the finding to their own diligence.
themes: a gift declared just after a search was commanded
a term confessed to be untranslatable
substance and advancement proposed for one word
protection and instruction competing in a single clause
a word for the devout traced into a party name

10.pericope_label: When wisdom entereth into thine heart: to deliver thee from the way of the evil man

schools.summary: Henry asks when wisdom can be said to have entire possession and answers by dominion and delight, holding that it must not merely fill the head with notions but enter the heart and work there as leaven in dough, diffusing its relish and changing the mass into its own image, and offers as a test that the tree is known by its fruits.

Gill reports the Greek version rendering the word for discretion as good counsel and offers a second sense in which discretion watches over a man, and notices that the word for leaving the paths of uprightness supposes these men to have been brought up in them, adding that though people do not easily leave the ways of their education, those who do are generally the worst of men.

Clarke takes the word for discretion in a good sense as a good device by which a man invents purposes of good, but prefers an older English version rendering the clause of counsel and calls it much better than the received one; he derives the froward things from a verb meaning to turn the course of a thing and makes the speakers seditious men who wish to subvert the civil or religious state, speak much of liberty and oppression and endeavour to corrupt the minds of youth. Wesley reduces the crooked ways to windings by which conviction is escaped.

Ellicott takes the tenth verse as an explanation of what precedes and would read for rather than when, renders the froward things as misrepresentations and distortions of the truth, and observes that the positive taking of pleasure in evil is named by an apostle as the last stage of degradation; Keil and Delitzsch read the conjunction the same way, treat the four terms as one continued subject, and gloss the same noun as misrepresentations of the good and true made for the purpose of deceiving.

debates: What does the man speak who utters froward things? Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both render the noun misrepresentations, that is, distortions of the good and the true made in order to deceive; Clarke derives it from a verb meaning to turn or change the course of a thing and makes it subversion, so that the men described are seditious and wish to make others so, speaking much of liberty and oppression, dealing in broad assertions and setting themselves especially to corrupt the minds of youth.
outliers: Clarke prefers an older English version’s rendering of the word for discretion, calling it a very good translation and much better than the received one; Gill independently reports the Greek version giving the same sense of counsel.

Henry holds that wisdom has entire possession only when it enters the heart and works there as leaven in dough, diffusing its relish and changing the mass into its own image, and not when it merely fills the head with notions.

Gill observes that the word for leaving the paths of uprightness supposes the men to have been brought up in them, and that those who abandon the ways of their education are generally the worst of men.
themes: a conjunction changed from when to for
possession of the heart distinguished from furnishing of the head
one word for a good device and for a wicked one
deceit and sedition proposed for the same noun
pleasure taken in evil counted the last stage

16.pericope_label: To deliver thee from the strange woman: for her house inclineth unto death

schools.summary: Gill denies that the woman is called strange for being of another nation and makes it that she belongs to another man, reports three allegorical readings and applies the passage to the corruptions of a church, canvasses God, parent and husband for the guide of her youth and settles on the husband, gives two constructions of the sinking house, and records that some of the ancients thought this sin unpardonable while insisting that some have been recovered.

Clarke alone takes the guide of her youth for the parent whose house and instructions are left, offers both apostasy and the marriage contract for the covenant, derives the flattering from a word meaning to smooth and claims an English verb descends from it, reads the house topographically as established off the high road so that every step toward it is a step toward death, and distinguishes two classes of fallen women in order to doubt whether the reformatory houses of his day can help the one while helping the other; Wesley keeps the covenant strictly to marriage and notes that God is called its author and witness.

Ellicott takes the two epithets to mean of another family and of another nation and builds on them a history in which the king’s foreign marriages set a common example and imported a laxer morality, reads the guide of her youth as the friend of her intimacy and first love, and renders the eighteenth verse that she sinks down with her house, house and all; Keil and Delitzsch reach the same distinction of the two epithets by philology, add that prostitution was partly sanctioned in neighbouring worship, explain how the allegorical reading of the adulteress arose, and suspect the Greek version of the eighteenth verse to be the original.

debates: What makes the woman strange? Ellicott holds the two epithets to mean of another family and of another nation, and infers a period in which foreign wives, following a royal example, imported a laxer morality; Keil and Delitzsch reach the same distinction philologically and add that prostitution was partly sanctioned in neighbouring worship though forbidden by the law; Gill denies the national sense outright and makes her strange only in belonging to another man.

Who is the guide of her youth? Gill canvasses God, her parent and her husband and settles on the husband, whom he calls the companion of her youth; Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch agree, the one calling him her first love and the other deriving the noun from a verb meaning to grow accustomed to a person; Clarke alone takes the parent, so that she leaves her father’s house and instructions.

How is the eighteenth verse to be construed? Gill gives the received sense and a second in which she inclines to death, which is her house; Ellicott renders it that she sinks down with her house, house and all, like the men the earth swallowed; Keil and Delitzsch report the Greek version making her set her house beside death, and suspect it may be the original since the received text is doubtful.
outliers: Clarke distinguishes women who fell by inclination from those who were deceived and abandoned, holds that the reformatory institutions of his day may help the second class while proving to the first only incentives to further sinning.
Keil and Delitzsch explain how the allegorical reading of the adulteress arose, since prophetic language about apostasy suggested to the old interpreters that she personifies apostasy or heresy.
Clarke claims that an English verb is descended from the Hebrew word for the woman’s smooth speech.
Gill records that some of the ancients thought this sin unpardonable, and answers that some have certainly been recovered, though an Aramaic version adds that they do not return in peace.
themes: two adjectives read as family and as nationality
a royal example blamed for a national corruption
a first companion variously made parent or husband
a house that sinks with its occupant
the possibility of return debated on the evidence
